name: Nasofrontal / nasolabial angle theory

lead: The nasofrontal angle is the angle at the nasion between the forehead and the nasal dorsum. The nasolabial angle is the angle between the columella and the upper lip under the nose. Both come from facial plastic surgery and orthodontic profile analysis, and looksmaxxing forums use them to measure how a nose looks from the side and decide what to change.

Surgical references give nasofrontal values of about 115 to 130 degrees, more acute in men (about 115 to 120) than in women (about 120 to 130), and nasolabial values of roughly 90 to 95 degrees in men and 100 to 105 in women. These serve as planning guides rather than strict standards.

paras: This is a measurement framework. Users read the angles from a side-profile photo or X-ray and compare their values with published ranges, in threads about brow ridge projection, bridge height and tip rotation. Changes are sought through rhinoplasty, brow-area implants or other procedures covered elsewhere.

The framework itself carries no direct risk. Ideal values vary between individuals, sexes and ethnic groups, and forum cut-offs are informal. Interventions discussed in connection with the angles, such as surgery, carry their own risks.

angle.text: Forum users borrow nasofrontal and nasolabial angle measurements from rhinoplasty and orthodontics to score side profiles and plan brow, nose or jaw changes. The angles are standard clinical measures, while the claim that they drive attractiveness comes mostly from community opinion.

lead: The nasofrontal angle and the nasolabial angle are two measurements of the nose in side view. The nasofrontal angle sits at the nasion between the line along the forehead (nasion to glabella) and the line along the nasal dorsum, while the nasolabial angle is formed between the columella and the line from the subnasale to the upper lip [1].

In surgical references, the nasofrontal angle is usually given as about 115 to 130 degrees, more acute in men (about 115 to 120) than in women (about 120 to 130), and the nasolabial angle as roughly 90 to 95 degrees in men and 100 to 105 in women [1]. These figures serve as planning guides rather than strict standards.
On looksmax.org and similar forums, the terms appear in threads about brow ridge projection, nasal bridge position and tip rotation, where users compare their own profiles with these ranges [2][3].
infobox: About 90 to 95 degrees men, 100 to 105 women [1]
Planning and forum scoring of nose profile

paras: The nasofrontal angle is measured between the nasion-to-nasal-tip line and the nasion-to-glabella line. A related nasofacial angle compares the nasal dorsum with a line to the pogonion and is typically about 30 to 40 degrees [1].

The nasolabial angle describes tip rotation and how the base of the nose meets the lip. It is also used in orthodontics, where profile-change studies examine how moving the upper front teeth alters the soft-tissue profile around the upper lip [1][4].

Forum threads treat a defined nasofrontal angle as part of a desirable side profile and link it to brow ridge prominence. One user describes planning supraorbital implants in the belief that they will improve the angle, and replies debate the relative importance of supraorbital and infraorbital recession [3]. Other threads ask whether counter-clockwise jaw rotation is needed when the nasolabial angle is already within the usual range, or what surgery changes the nasolabial angle.
These threads reflect how members describe goals and procedures. They are individual opinions and questions rather than clinical findings.

No studies found on the forum use of these angles as a rating framework. Related research exists in orthodontics and craniofacial surgery: a cephalometric comparison of Japanese and European-American adults with well-balanced faces examined how profile measurements differ by population [5], and cephalometric studies of orthodontic and surgical movements report soft-tissue profile changes around the lip and nose [4][6].

lore.intro: Members of looksmax.org use nasofrontal and nasolabial angle values as shorthand when evaluating profiles and planning procedures [3].

claims.claim: A good nasofrontal angle is a key part of an attractive side profile.
Brow-ridge implants or brow augmentation can improve a poor nasofrontal angle.
The nasolabial angle should be ideal, and its surgical correction or jaw movement is part of an ascension plan.
